While brainstorming better mechanisms for indicating AI agent workflows, I was thinking that it would be nice if I could really quickly select between predefined workflows for individual agents.

What if there was a concise Markup Language that, like Markdown, both described and visually resembled a Web/Form you wanted to see and fill out, and thereby implied and expressed the underlying Schema of the form?

Mermaid Diagrams and similar syntax-based diagrams don't tend to be that human-readable or writeable. They feel like programming; there are too many pointers for it to be casually written and read without very detailed practice.

There are also schema languages like JSON Schema and Pydantic, but again, those are for a very strict subset of users, and I'm not sure they are the best way to casually represent what amounts to user queries.

But if there was a Markup Language like Markdown which could represent a human-readable schema of a Web/Form, disassociated from its presentation, such that I could open up a TUI preview in nvim where I could get fuzzy autocomplete on the select drop-downs and quickly be able to fill in text boxes where I had a full vim buffer, and it would end up producing a really nicely formatted document? AI/Agent/Harnesses could do generative TUI in a way that went beyond simple question answer. Of course, one could just use HTML for this, too. That's probably the simpler idea. But I love my CLIs and TUIs, and CLIs and TUIs can go places that HTML can't, but the opposite is true as well. If there was an intermediate markup language that could render to multiple formats and was also quite readable and writeable by hand, that could be quite useful.

A form of SSO offered to friends and family, so that different people can be granted access to different parts of a personal and family site without being told in advance.

The sign-up form asks a series of questions that, one after another, establish who the person is and how they know the site's owner, without giving anything away, until their closeness is established.
Accounts can be granted before a person creates one, and the person can choose whether to take it, like telling the concierge of a building, "if you ever see this person, let them in."
Once a visitor is signed in, they can reply to what they see at any time.

Soft Hashes for Lazy Vector Indexing

Let agents decide at retrieval time whether a corpus needs vector search, instead of precomputing embeddings for every possible use. Lazy indexing avoids spending compute and disk on retrieval patterns no agent may need, and avoids baking those assumptions into the corpus in advance.
Soft Hashes for Lazy Vector Indexing

Give each document or chunk a stable address, in the spirit of IPFS, and compute an inexpensive soft hash when the chunk is first indexed. The soft hash would act as a fast proxy for whether the stored vector still represents the current text.
Soft Hashes for Lazy Vector Indexing

On a later vector retrieval, compare the current chunk's soft hash with the one associated with its vector. If the change is significant, return the available result with a freshness signal and queue a re-embedding asynchronously; if it is still a close enough proxy, reuse the vector.
Soft Hashes for Lazy Vector Indexing

A shared store for a team's corpus could let machines reuse existing chunk identities, freshness metadata, and vectors instead of independently embedding the same content. Agents could request vector indexing only when useful, while later users benefit from the work already done.
Soft Hashes for Lazy Vector Indexing

The hard part is defining the soft hash and its threshold: it must be cheap to compute, sensitive to meaning-changing edits, and tolerant of changes that do not make the old embedding misleading. It may relate to the embedding itself, but should be cheaper than recomputing the embedding.
Soft Hashes for Lazy Vector Indexing

Open questions: How should chunk identity survive edits or changed chunk boundaries? How should freshness be represented across embedding models and versions? Can the store coordinate deduplication and asynchronous refresh across machines without making a central service mandatory?
Soft Hashes for Lazy Vector Indexing
This connects to AI/Embedding and the question of when AI/Agents should choose indexed retrieval over direct search.

Every time I start a repository, I write agent instructions explaining how issues are prioritized, what "blocked by" means, how parent and child work is modeled, and how all of that maps onto whichever tracker the repository uses: GitHub/Issue, JIRA, Beads, or maybe Linear. The meanings barely change from project to project. Only the tracker mechanics change.

What if a small, provider-neutral Schema defined what the terms mean, and a separate binding per tracker said how each term is represented there? An agent could read the schema and know what priority and dependencies mean without knowing which tracker is in use.
A handful of concepts: work item, status, priority, blocks / blocked-by, parent / child, and relates-to. Maybe milestone.
Each concept carries a short definition a human can read and approve.
A binding maps each concept onto one tracker's fields:
In JIRA, high maps to the native Priority field and blocks to the Blocks link type. In Beads, both are native.
A small CLI could read the binding, set up the tracker (create missing labels, check that link types exist), and report mismatches, the way infrastructure-as-code tools treat cloud resources.
The repository holds the schema and the bindings. The tracker holds the issues themselves.
A repository-specific skill could then shrink to a few lines: read the schema, use the CLI.

OSLC Change Management Version 3.0 from OASIS defines change requests and their relationships. It is the closest existing standard, but no mainstream tracker uses it as its native model. Its vocabulary could inform the names in the schema.
Should priority, severity, and urgency be separate concepts, or should the core carry only priority and leave the others to an optional profile?
How should a binding carry tracker-specific fields, such as Jira story points, without adding them to the core?
Should backlog maintenance (finding duplicates, missing dependencies, stale or orphaned work) be defined as standard operations alongside the data?

OpenSpec makes a change the unit of work, which suits brownfield projects: no one has to specify the whole system first. But a long run of changes, each sensible on its own, can carry a project away from what it was for, because nothing in the repository says what it was for. Today I supply that context from this garden, so an agent working only in the repository doesn't have it.
What if a project had a standard place for its why: its vision, goals, Principles, and constraints, which change proposals and issues could cite?
What changes: change proposals and requirements, as in OpenSpec.
What work: issues, priority, dependencies, as in Idea/Standard/Project/Management/Schema.
Where the work is stored: the binding to GitHub/Issue, JIRA, Beads, or another tracker.

A change proposal would name the goals and principles it serves, and a work item would name the change it implements, so the reason for a piece of work can be traced back without searching old conversations.
What problem the project solves, who it is for, what it leaves out, and what success looks like.
Principles pile up: some apply everywhere, others only to security, data, or UI work. A single principles.md grows long, and most of it is irrelevant to any one change.

Splitting principles by area behind a short index gives Progressive Disclosure: an agent changing authentication reads the vision, the security principles, the auth constraints, and the relevant ADRs, and skips the rest.
Each principle could carry tags or an applies-when condition, so a tool can pick the relevant ones for a change.
A small manifest at the repository root would point to each piece, so a project can keep its own folder layout.
GitHub/SpecKit has a constitution that holds a project's principles above its specs and plans. It doesn't cover the problem, the audience, or what success looks like.
arc42 is an architecture documentation template that keeps goals, constraints, context, quality requirements, and decisions in separate sections.
What is the smallest set of concepts that lets a person and an agent agree on why a project exists and which rules govern a change?
Choosing a profile for a new project should feel like choosing the MIT license or adopting Conventional Commits. What would the default profile contain?
